column1: In model theory, what fundamental question distinguishes it from proof theory?
column2: Proof theory asks what theorems can be syntactically derived from axioms; model theory asks what it means for a statement to be semantically true in a particular mathematical structure.

column1: What are the three core components that define a first-order structure $\mathcal{M}$ for a signature $\sigma$?
column2: A nonempty domain set $M$, plus interpretations for each symbol in $\sigma$: specific elements for constants, specific functions for function symbols, and specific relations for relation symbols.

column1: Who established the compositional (recursive) definition of truth/satisfaction for formal languages, and why was this historically significant?
column2: Alfred Tarski (1930s). It broke the apparent circularity of defining truth by building satisfaction recursively from atomic formulas up through connectives and quantifiers, turning 'truth' into a precise mathematical relation.

column1: Define $\mathrm{Th}(\mathcal{M})$, the theory of a structure $\mathcal{M}$.
column2: $$\mathrm{Th}(\mathcal{M}) = \{\varphi \in \mathcal{L}(\sigma) : \mathcal{M} \models \varphi,\ \varphi \text{ a sentence}\}$$ — the complete set of first-order sentences true in $\mathcal{M}$.

column1: What does it mean for two structures $\mathcal{M}$ and $\mathcal{N}$ to be elementarily equivalent ($\mathcal{M} \equiv \mathcal{N}$), and how does this relate to isomorphism?
column2: $\mathrm{Th}(\mathcal{M}) = \mathrm{Th}(\mathcal{N})$, i.e., every sentence true in one is true in the other. Isomorphism implies elementary equivalence, but the converse fails (e.g., $\mathbb{R}$ vs. a non-Archimedean real-closed field).

column1: What is a complete theory $T$, and what unique property do all its models share?
column2: $T$ is complete if for every sentence $\varphi$, either $T \models \varphi$ or $T \models \neg\varphi$ (no sentence is undecided). Consequently, all models of $T$ are elementarily equivalent to one another.

column1: State the Gödel Completeness Theorem's equivalence used to prove Compactness.
column2: A set of sentences $\Gamma$ is satisfiable if and only if it is consistent (no contradiction derivable via first-order proof rules). This syntactic/semantic equivalence underlies the proof of the Compactness Theorem.

column1: State the Compactness Theorem for first-order logic.
column2: A set of first-order sentences $\Gamma$ has a model if and only if every finite subset of $\Gamma$ has a model.

column1: State the Downward and Upward Löwenheim-Skolem Theorems.
column2: Downward: any theory with an infinite model has a countable model. Upward: any theory with an infinite model has models of arbitrarily large cardinality.

column1: What striking consequence do the Löwenheim-Skolem theorems have for Peano Arithmetic (PA)?
column2: They imply the existence of non-standard models of PA: models satisfying all first-order axioms of PA yet containing elements ('nonstandard integers') different from the standard natural numbers.

column1: What does it mean for a theory $T$ to admit quantifier elimination?
column2: Every formula $\phi(\bar{x})$ is logically equivalent modulo $T$ to a quantifier-free formula $\psi(\bar{x})$ in the same free variables, meaning definable sets reduce to Boolean combinations of atomic formulas.

column1: Give Tarski's classic example of quantifier elimination in real closed fields, and define model completeness.
column2: $\exists x\,(x^2+bx+c=0)$ in $(\mathbb{R},+,\cdot,0,1,<)$ reduces to the quantifier-free condition $b^2-4c \ge 0$. A theory is model complete if every embedding between its models is elementary, equivalent to every formula being equivalent to an existential formula (weaker than full quantifier elimination).
